Module 1.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary • 24MEP602 Module 1
📐 Core Governing Equations
  • 2D Translation Matrix: $[T] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ t_x & t_y & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ (in row-vector convention)
  • 2D Rotation About Origin Matrix: $[R] = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
  • 2D Scaling Matrix: $[S] = \begin{bmatrix} s_x & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
  • Rotation About Arbitrary Point $(x_p, y_p)$: $[T_{\text{composite}}] = [T(-x_p, -y_p)] \cdot [R(\theta)] \cdot [T(x_p, y_p)]$
📌 Essential Concepts & Rules
  • Why Homogeneous Coordinates?: Adds an extra dimension (weight factor $w=1$) allowing translation, rotation, and scaling to all be expressed as uniform matrix multiplications.
  • Matrix Concatenation: Combines multiple sequential transformations into single $3 \times 3$ (2D) or $4 \times 4$ (3D) composite matrix, avoiding per-vertex repeated calculations.
💡 2-Minute Exam Revision Tips
  • Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative: $[T] \cdot [R] \ne [R] \cdot [T]$.
  • In 3D, rotation can occur about $X, Y,$ or $Z$ axes with right-hand rule convention.
Module 1.detailed_notes:
Comprehensive Engineering Analysis • Geometric Modeling Mathematics & Graphic Pipelines

1. Coordinate Transformations & Projection Geometry

Computer graphics pipelines transform CAD models from Local Model Coordinates -> World Coordinates -> Camera/Eye Coordinates -> Normalized Device Coordinates -> Screen Pixels using concatenated 4x4 affine matrix operators.

$$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ z' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & r_{12} & r_{13} & t_x \\ r_{21} & r_{22} & r_{23} & t_y \\ r_{31} & r_{32} & r_{33} & t_z \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
🛠️ Engineering Application: CAD graphics rendering engines (AutoCAD, SolidWorks, CATIA) and game engine 3D viewports.

Module 2.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary • 24MEP602 Module 2
📐 Core Governing Equations
  • Bézier Curve Formula: $\mathbf{P}(u) = \sum_{i=0}^n B_{i,n}(u) \mathbf{P}_i$ ($0 \le u \le 1$, where $\mathbf{P}_i$ are control points)
  • Bernstein Polynomials: $B_{i,n}(u) = \binom{n}{i} u^i (1 - u)^{n - i}$
  • Convex Hull Property: The Bézier curve lies entirely within the convex hull formed by its control polygon.
  • B-Spline Advantage: Provides local control: moving a single control point alters only adjacent segments without disturbing entire curve.
📌 Essential Concepts & Rules
  • Hermite vs Bézier: Hermite requires end points and tangent vectors; Bézier defines shape purely using control points.
  • Continuity Levels: $C^0$ (positional continuity - curve connects); $C^1$ (tangent vector continuous); $C^2$ (radius of curvature continuous).
💡 2-Minute Exam Revision Tips
  • Bézier curve passes through FIRST and LAST control points ($P_0$ and $P_n$); intermediate points attract the curve without touching.
  • NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines) can represent both freeform sculptured shapes and exact conic sections (circles, ellipses).
Module 2.detailed_notes:
Comprehensive Engineering Analysis • Parametric Curve Formulations & Surface Modeling

1. Synthetic Curves & Blending Function Formulations

Parametric curve representations avoid infinite slope singularities of explicit equations ($y=f(x)$). Bernstein basis functions satisfy partition of unity $\sum B_{i,n}(u) = 1$, ensuring affine invariance.

$$\mathbf{P}(u) = (1-u)^3 \mathbf{P}_0 + 3u(1-u)^2 \mathbf{P}_1 + 3u^2(1-u) \mathbf{P}_2 + u^3 \mathbf{P}_3, \quad \mathbf{P}'(0) = 3(\mathbf{P}_1 - \mathbf{P}_0)$$
🛠️ Engineering Application: Aerodynamic automotive body styling (Class A surfacing) and aircraft wing lofting.

Module 3.title: Solid Modeling: CSG, B-Rep & CAD Data Exchange
Module 3.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 500 130" style="width:100%; max-width:480px; height:auto; background:#0f172a; border-radius:8px; padding:10px; margin:10px auto; display:block;"><text x="20" y="25" fill="#38bdf8" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) Tree & Boolean Operators</text><text x='110' y='75' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='14'>Block ∪ Cylinder (Union) • Solid ∩ Tool (Intersection) • Block - Hole (Difference)</text></svg>
Module 3.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary • 24MEP602 Module 3
📐 Core Governing Equations
  • Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG): Represents solids as binary tree of primitive shapes (block, cylinder, sphere, cone) combined via Boolean operations (Union $\cup$, Difference $-$, Intersection $\cap$).
  • Boundary Representation (B-Rep): Defines solid by its bounding topological entities (Faces, Edges, Vertices) and geometric surfaces/curves.
  • Euler-Poincaré Formula: $V - E + F - H = 2(S - G)$ (for polyhedra with holes $H$, bodies $S$, passages/genus $G$)
📌 Essential Concepts & Rules
  • CAD Exchange Formats: STEP (ISO 10303 - standard for product model data), IGES (Initial graphics exchange), STL (triangulated mesh for 3D printing).
  • Medical CAD Modeling: Converting DICOM CT/MRI 3D voxel scans into CAD parametric solids for surgical planning.
💡 2-Minute Exam Revision Tips
  • CSG is always geometrically unambiguous and valid; B-Rep requires topological consistency checks.
  • STEP AP203/AP214 is the industry standard format preserving design intent and assembly hierarchies across different CAD vendors.
Module 3.detailed_notes:
Comprehensive Engineering Analysis • Solid Modeling Architectures & Interoperability

1. Topology vs Geometry in Modern Solid Modelers

B-Rep stores topological connectivity in half-edge or winged-edge data structures linked to analytical underlying NURBS surfaces. CSG trees enable parametric feature replay and direct geometry modification.

$$\text{Euler Equation: } V - E + F = 2 \quad (\text{Simple closed solid})$$
🛠️ Engineering Application: Complex casting core box design, multi-axis CNC toolpath verification, and patient-specific orthopedic implants.

<svg viewBox="0 0 500 150" style="width:100%; max-width:480px; height:auto; background:#0f172a; border:1px solid #334155; border-radius:8px; padding:10px; margin:10px auto; display:block;">

  <line x1="108" y1="75" x2="280" y2="75" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="4"/>

</svg>
Module 4.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary • 24MEP602 Module 4
📐 Core Governing Equations
  • Global Governing FEM Equation: $\{F\} = [K] \{u\}$ (where $[K]$ is global assembled stiffness matrix, $\{u\}$ nodal displacements)
  • 1D Bar Element Stiffness Matrix: $[k] = \frac{A E}{L} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
  • Shape Functions (Linear 1D Bar): $N_1(x) = 1 - \frac{x}{L}, N_2(x) = \frac{x}{L}$ (Displacement $u(x) = N_1 u_1 + N_2 u_2$)
  • Strain-Displacement Matrix ($[B]$): $[B] = \frac{d[N]}{dx} = \begin{bmatrix} -\frac{1}{L} & \frac{1}{L} \end{bmatrix}$, Strain $\varepsilon = [B] \{u\}$, Stress $\sigma = E [B] \{u\}$
📌 Essential Concepts & Rules
  • Element Stiffness Formulation: $[k] = \int_V [B]^T [D] [B] dV$, where $[D]$ is material elasticity matrix.
  • Boundary Conditions Treatment: Elimination method (delete rows/cols of fixed DOFs) vs Penalty method (add large spring stiffness $C$).
💡 2-Minute Exam Revision Tips
  • Stiffness matrix $[K]$ is always symmetric, banded, and positive semi-definite (becomes positive definite after applying boundary conditions).
  • Convergence requires shape functions to satisfy completeness (rigid body motion, constant strain) and compatibility across inter-element boundaries.
Module 4.detailed_notes:
Comprehensive Engineering Analysis • Finite Element Formulations & Computational Mechanics

1. Principle of Minimum Potential Energy & Rayleigh-Ritz Method

For a stable elastic structure, total potential energy $\Pi = U - W$ is stationary with respect to admissible kinematically admissible virtual displacement variations $\delta \Pi = 0$. Discretizing the continuum into finite elements converts differential equations into linear algebraic systems.

$$\Pi = \frac{1}{2} \{u\}^T [K] \{u\} - \{u\}^T \{F\}, \quad \frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial \{u\}} = 0 \implies [K]\{u\} = \{F\}$$
🛠️ Engineering Application: Structural crashworthiness simulation, aerospace fuselage stress verification, and turbine thermal-stress analysis.

Module 5.title: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) & Structural Optimization
Module 5.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 500 130" style="width:100%; max-width:480px; height:auto; background:#0f172a; border-radius:8px; padding:10px; margin:10px auto; display:block;"><text x="20" y="25" fill="#38bdf8" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">CFD Navier-Stokes Discretization & Mesh Boundary</text><text x='80' y='75' fill='#38bdf8' font-size='13'>Continuity + Momentum (Navier-Stokes) + Energy → FVM Discretization → Solver Convergence</text></svg>
Module 5.short_notes:
⚡ High-Yield Exam Summary • 24MEP602 Module 5
📐 Core Governing Equations
  • Navier-Stokes Momentum Equation: $\rho \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{v} \right) = -\nabla p + \mu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} + \rho \mathbf{g}$
  • Finite Volume Method (FVM): Discretizes integral conservation laws over control volumes; inherently guarantees strict conservation of mass, momentum, and energy.
  • Topology Optimization: Material distribution algorithm (SIMP method) that redistributes material density $\rho_i$ ($0 \le \rho_i \le 1$) to maximize stiffness for target weight.
📌 Essential Concepts & Rules
  • Mesh Quality Metrics: Aspect ratio, Orthogonal quality ($>0.15$), Skewness ($<0.85$), Wall $y^+$ spacing for turbulence boundary layers.
  • Boundary Conditions in CFD: Velocity inlet, Pressure outlet, No-slip wall, Periodic/Symmetry planes.
💡 2-Minute Exam Revision Tips
  • Low $y^+$ ($y^+ < 1$) resolves viscous sublayer directly (enhanced wall treatment).
  • Topology optimization generates organic, bionic structural shapes ideal for additive manufacturing.
Module 5.detailed_notes:
Comprehensive Engineering Analysis • CFD Simulation & Modern Generative Design

1. Numerical Fluid Solvers & Topology Optimization Algorithms

CFD numerical schemes discretize convective and diffusive flux terms using upwind/central differencing coupled via SIMPLE/PISO pressure-velocity coupling algorithms.

$$\min_{\rho_e} \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{U}^T \mathbf{K} \mathbf{U} \quad \text{subject to } \sum \rho_e V_e \le V^*, \quad E_e(\rho_e) = \rho_e^p E_0$$
🛠️ Engineering Application: Formula 1 aerodynamic front wing downforce optimization, electronic heatsink natural convection, and lightweight aerospace brackets.
